summary: Discovery with Helios Retail to understand latency (p95), concurrency, streaming behavior and throughput (tokens/sec). Helios needs sub-300ms p95 on short chat completions at ~50 concurrent users and plans for 200 concurrency bursts. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, KV/prefix cache, quantization and benchmarking plan. Agreed to run two benchmark passes and share pricing + security docs. Next step technical deep-dive for private deployment if benchmarks look good.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Javier Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Javier from Redwood, AE on this account. with me is Priya, our SE. good to meet you all.
[00:08] Mark Reynolds: Hey Javier, thanks. I'm Mark, CTO at Helios. we've got Sophie, Liam and Asha on too.
[00:14] Priya Mehta: great. quick agenda - we want to understand your latency targets, concurrency patterns, whether you'll use streaming, and then we can propose hosted vs dedicated vs private options and a benchmark plan. sound good?
[00:24] Mark Reynolds: yeah that's perfect. to give context - Helios runs low-latency shopping assistant across mobile and web - a lot of short chat completions, some longer summarization offline. main concern is p95 on interactive chat. target for the product team is ~200-300ms p95 for short responses (under 60 tokens). we also need to handle 50 steady concurrent users and spikes up to 200 concurrent for promos.
[00:44] Priya Mehta: ok that's useful. when you say 50 concurrent users, is that 50 simultaneous streams or 50 requests per second?
[00:50] Sophie Chen: it's users, so often streaming websockets — so we'd have 50 live streams, each sending a few tokens at a time; burst events could create 200 concurrent live streams. average prompt is pretty short, median 35 tokens in, 40 tokens out.
[01:04] Javier Ortiz: got it. are you currently using any provider or self-hosted infra?
[01:08] Mark Reynolds: we started with a managed API from a big vendor (we won't name names), but cost and burst predictability are issues. exploring dedicated capacity or private to control latency/cost. security teams will need SOC2 docs, audit logs, and KMS integration.
[01:22] Priya Mehta: that's common. for p95 ~200-300ms on short streaming responses, a few levers matter: model size/opt, batching behavior, streaming chunk sizes, and whether you have KV/prefix caching for repeated user context. Redwood Dedicated gives you predictable GPU pools and can hit sub-200ms p95 on optimized small models for that token size. hosted can also hit it but depends on concurrency and burst policy.
[01:40] Liam Patel: can you clarify that - hosted can hit sub-200ms but depends on burst policy? what do you mean?
[01:45] Evan Liu: right so hosted is multi-tenant; we have autoscaling and burst capacity but heavy bursts can incur queueing or fallback to slightly larger latency models. Dedicated provides reserved GPU throughput so you get more consistent tail latency. in hosted we also do smart routing and fallback to model variants.
[01:58] Mark Reynolds: okay. do you have concrete token/sec numbers and p95 numbers we can use for planning? we need to quantify cost vs commit.
[02:05] Priya Mehta: yes. ballpark for a properly optimized 7B-ish model with quantization and streaming, on our Dedicated pools you might see p95 ~120-220ms for sub-60-token responses at 50 concurrency. tokens/sec sustained per GPU will vary — roughly 4k-10k tokens/sec per A100-equivalent for small models depending on batch efficiency and kv cache hit rate. hosted numbers are similar on average but can have wider variance at tail.
[02:27] Sophie Chen: that 120-220ms p95 is for streaming right? and does that include network RTT?
[02:31] Priya Mehta: that's server-side generation p95; add network RTT — on our hosted region closer to your users it's typically an extra 20-50ms. streaming latency can look a bit different because partial tokens are delivered as chunks — first token can be lower latency but full response p95 is measured on final token.
[02:45] Asha Kapoor: we also use some reranking for product search responses — that adds a second model call sometimes. how do you recommend architecting that without exceeding p95?
[02:53] Evan Liu: common pattern is to do fast coarse generation on a small model + cached reranker or on-device filter, and only call the large reranker asynchronously for enrichment. we also support batching and async callbacks so your critical path can be kept below SLO.
[03:06] Mark Reynolds: good. what about concurrency math — if we have 50 live streams and each stream produces tokens roughly every 200ms, what's the effective tokens/sec we need to provision for?
[03:15] Priya Mehta: quick calc — 50 streams * tokens per second per stream. if each stream emits 3 tokens/sec (rough avg) that's 150 tokens/sec; for 200 streams that's 600 tokens/sec. but tokens/sec alone isn't the whole story — p95 depends on spikes and sequencing of requests, and whether you're doing long sequences that hold the kv cache.
[03:33] Sophie Chen: our average tokens per request is 40 out, so on a per-request basis at 50 concurrent you get different load profiles. we can share sample logs.
[03:40] Javier Ortiz: yes please share logs and sample prompt sets — that'll help Priya run the benchmark with realistic weights.
[03:45] Liam Patel: on the private/on-prem side, our security team prefers to see KMS integration and ability to audit key usage. is that supported?
[03:52] Priya Mehta: yes, Private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM and full audit logs. we can provide SOC 2 materials and runbook for VPC peering. there will be some operational overhead on Helios side for network and firewall setup.
[04:04] Mark Reynolds: another concern is quantization. we want to reduce cost but maintain quality at high concurrency. what quantization profiles do you suggest?
[04:12] Priya Mehta: for many models, 4-bit quant can be good with careful calibration, but for very latency-sensitive small responses we often recommend 8-bit or mixed 8/4 profiles to preserve quality. Redwood Optimize includes recommendations and we can run evals to compare quality vs latency.
[04:27] Sophie Chen: will you run token/sec benchmarks for both streaming and non-streaming? streaming is critical for us.
[04:31] Priya Mehta: yes we'll do both. benchmark plan I propose: run 1) streaming scenario with your prompt set at 50 concurrent steady state and 2) burst scenario up to 200 concurrency for 5-minute window; measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec and per-token costs. we'll run hosted and dedicated runs.
[04:46] Mark Reynolds: sounds good. what's the expected time to get benchmark results back?
[04:49] Javier Ortiz: Priya, feasible timeframe?
[04:51] Priya Mehta: assuming we get prompt set and sample logs today, i can run initial passes and share results in ~5 business days. we'll iterate if we need different models or quant settings.
[04:59] Asha Kapoor: any considerations for streaming chunk size — we've seen that using smaller chunks reduces latency but increases overhead.
[05:06] Evan Liu: yes chunk size matters. smaller chunks give faster first bytes but can increase compute overhead per token. there's a balance; we can test 1-2 token chunk vs 4-8 token chunks. also websocket latency and TLS negotiation matter — keep connections warm.
[05:20] Liam Patel: on dedicated vs hosted pricing — can you summarize the tradeoffs quickly?
[05:24] Javier Ortiz: sure. hosted is usage-based, easiest to start, but tail latency and burst predictability can vary; dedicated gives reserved throughput and more predictable p95 at scale with monthly/annual commit and better isolation; private adds customer-managed network and KMS for the highest control and compliance but with more ops work. pricing for dedicated depends on committed GPUs and burst allowances. I'll share a pricing sheet after this call.
[05:43] Mark Reynolds: do you support A/B routing so we can test a cheaper quantized model on a fraction of traffic?
[05:47] Priya Mehta: yes Redwood supports rollouts/canary/A-B and automatic fallback policies. you can route by route or user cohort and collect per-route latency/cost metrics in the Console.
[05:56] Sophie Chen: for the benchmarks, can you include model variants — 7B raw, 7B quant 4-bit, 13B quant 8-bit, and maybe a distilled 3B?
[06:02] Priya Mehta: yes we'll include those; helps to understand cost/latency/quality tradeoffs.
[06:07] Mark Reynolds: on audit and compliance — we need to ensure logs show prompt-level access and admin governance.
[06:12] Priya Mehta: Private supports fine-grained audit logs and integrations with your SIEM. Hosted also provides audit logs and RBAC but Private gives you full control of the logs' retention and location.
[06:22] Asha Kapoor: do you have an example runbook for a dedicated deployment? operations-wise what do we expect?
[06:27] Evan Liu: yes we'll share a runbook — shows peering steps, certificate rotation, KMS config, and SLO alerting. operations are lighter for hosted, heavier for private but you gain control.
[06:37] Mark Reynolds: what's usually the biggest surprise for customers during onboarding?
[06:41] Javier Ortiz: often it's prompt engineering and caching — customers are surprised how much cost and latency you can save by prefix caching and aggressive batching for non-interactive paths. also monitoring and evals catch regressions early.
[06:53] Sophie Chen: ok - hypothetical numbers: if we want p95 < 250ms end-to-end for 50 concurrent streaming users, what's the minimal committed dedicated footprint to start with?
[07:02] Priya Mehta: rough rule: for short responses, a 4-GPU dedicated pool of A100-equivalent with optimized model should handle 50 concurrent streams comfortably with p95 under 250ms, assuming efficient batching and caching. but we'll validate with benchmarks using your data — that's why we want your prompt set and concurrency profile.
[07:19] Mark Reynolds: and cost roughly?
[07:21] Javier Ortiz: i'll share ranges in the pricing doc — depends on region and commitment. hosted usage cost for that throughput might be higher in steady-state. dedicated amortizes with commit.
[07:30] Sophie Chen: can we also test long-form summarization latency? those aren't in the interactive SLO but affect cost for background jobs.
[07:35] Priya Mehta: yes we'll include a non-interactive long-form job run to show tokens/sec sustained and cost per summary.
[07:42] Liam Patel: on network — we need to know average egress bandwidth for sustained tokens/sec so we can size peering.
[07:48] Evan Liu: we can include bandwidth numbers in the benchmark report — tokens/sec maps to bytes/sec depending on encoding and chunking. we'll give conservative estimates.
[07:57] Mark Reynolds: any gotchas for streaming in browsers vs mobile?
[08:01] Priya Mehta: TLS and connection keepalive are important; mobile networks have higher variance, so buffering at the client side and smaller chunks help. also consider using CDN edge for static assets to reduce RTT.
[08:12] Asha Kapoor: ok let's recap next steps.
[08:15] Javier Ortiz: recap: Helios will send prompt set and sample traffic logs, Redwood will run hosted + dedicated benchmarks (streaming + non-streaming, burst profile), Redwood to send pricing and security docs, schedule deep-dive if benchmarks look good.
[08:28] Mark Reynolds: that matches. thanks all.
[08:31] Priya Mehta: thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the benchmark plan doc.
[08:35] Sophie Chen: thanks everyone.
[08:36] End of recording.
